analysis.one_liner: Strips members of Congress of federal pensions, automatic pay raises, and taxpayer-funded perks.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The Citizen Congress Act would have taken away a list of benefits that members of Congress get: their place in the federal pension systems, automatic pay raises and pension increases, free flights on military planes, care at military hospitals, taxpayer-funded mass mailings, and free reserved airport parking. It also would have required a recorded vote on any congressional pay raise and forced public disclosure of each member's estimated pension. The bill was referred to a Senate committee and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers benefit, because the public would no longer fund congressional pensions under the same civil-service systems federal workers use, automatic pay raises and annuity increases, frequent-flier perks, military aircraft travel, military-hospital care, mass franked mailings, and reserved free parking at Washington-area airports. Ordinary voters would also see a published estimate of each member's future pension.

how_it_helps.text: Removes members of Congress from the Civil Service Retirement System and the Federal Employees' Retirement System, letting them use the Thrift Savings Plan for at most 12 years instead, while preserving pensions already earned from prior service.
Requires public disclosure of each member's retirement contributions and an estimate of the annuity each member would receive, so voters can compute the pension value of a congressional career.
Eliminates automatic cost-of-living increases for the congressional portion of member annuities and repeals the automatic pay adjustment for members.
Requires a roll call vote — a recorded, name-by-name vote — before any matter affecting congressional pay can be decided, so members cannot raise their own pay silently.
Bars members from using frequent-flier miles and other travel rewards earned on official trips for personal travel.
States that members may not send mass mailings as franked (postage-free) mail, ending a taxpayer-funded channel for self-promotion to constituents.

Restricts members' use of Military Air Command aircraft to cases where commercial flights are unavailable or the military flight is demonstrably the cheapest option, and bars members from receiving routine medical or dental care at military facilities unless they independently qualify for it.
Ends free reserved parking for members, other officials, and diplomats at Washington National and Dulles airports and directs the airports authority to give the public equal access.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress pay, by losing their federal pension participation, automatic pay raises and annuity increases, frequent-flier miles earned on official trips, free military flights and military medical care, franked mass mailings, and free reserved airport parking. Existing pensions already earned would be preserved.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress, out of perks

drawbacks.text: The bill grandfathers benefits already earned: pensions based on service before enactment are preserved, and members receiving military flights or medical care on the date of enactment can finish their current travel or care, so any immediate savings would be limited and the full effect would take decades.

Ending federal pension participation and automatic pay adjustments could make congressional service financially less attractive, an argument opponents could raise about recruiting qualified candidates.

Several provisions, such as the airport parking rule, are small in dollar terms, and the mass-mailing ban is written as a statement of congressional intent rather than a flat prohibition, which would invite testing of its limits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to taxpayers is real but modest: congressional pensions, pay raises, flights, mail, and parking are a small share of the federal budget, and the bill's grandfathering would delay most of the savings for years. The main value is symbolic and structural — making members pay their own way and record their pay-raise votes — and the bill is straightforwardly designed, with clear exemptions for emergencies and commercially inaccessible destinations. Against that, the cost falls entirely on the 535 people who would have to vote to impose it on themselves, and none of them chose to move it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to a Senate committee the day it was introduced and never came up again, dying when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Frist introduced the Citizen Congress Act on November 8, 1995, to eliminate certain benefits for Members of Congress.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Governmental Affairs the day it was introduced.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded — and the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting members of Congress came out ahead: every benefit the bill would have taken away — pensions, automatic raises, military flights, military medical care, franked mailings, and free airport parking — remained in place, at public expense. Taxpayers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Bill Frist
for.role: U.S. Senator from Tennessee, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Sen. Ted Stevens
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat in committee until the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Republicans and no vote was ever taken, so no party split shows up in the record; the bill simply died in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have ended members' federal pension participation, automatic pay and annuity increases, military flights and medical care, mass franked mailings, and free airport parking. Because the bill died without any action, incumbents kept all of these benefits at public expense.
